data.heading: Key Terms and Concepts
bullets: Repression: a policy of terror with 4 phases in Uzbekistan (1920s-early 1930s, 1936-1939, 1946-1953, 1983-1985)
The Great Terror: the phase of 1936-1939 where >70% of leaders were repressed by spring 1938
Troika of the NKVD: a three-person tribunal for 'counter-revolutionary' affairs
Milliy Istiqlol: the underground organization 'National Independence' (arrests of late 1929, head Munavvar Qari)
Milliy E'tiqod: the movement 'National Faith'; members were sentenced to death or long terms
Deculturation: the destruction of national culture through changing writing and imposing Soviet rites

narr: Let's begin with the concept of repression, which was implemented in four distinct phases in Uzbekistan.
The most severe of these was the Great Terror from 1936 to 1939, which saw over 70% of leaders repressed by 1938.
During this period, special tribunals called 'Troikas' were established to handle 'counter-revolutionary' cases.
Underground resistance movements like Milliy Istiqlol, or National Independence, emerged, though they were quickly suppressed.
Similarly, the Milliy E'tiqod movement, or National Faith, faced severe consequences with members receiving death sentences or long prison terms.
The Soviet policy of deculturation aimed to destroy national identity by changing writing systems and imposing Soviet cultural practices.

data.heading: Soviet Cultural Policies and Deportations
bullets: Korenizatsiya: the advancement of local cadres in the early 1920s, curtailed by the end of the 1920s
'Socialist in content...': the cultural formula of 'socialist in content, internationalist in spirit, national in form'
Cyrillisation of 1940: the introduction of Cyrillic script for Uzbek language by decree
Deportations: 74,500 Koreans (1937), ~110,000 Meskhetian Turks, 151,424 Crimean Tatars (1943-1944)
Evacuation: housing of >100 enterprises and 1 million people (including 200,000 children) in 1941-1942
Hero of the Soviet Union: the highest title awarded to 280 people from Uzbekistan, 75 of whom were Uzbeks

narr: The Soviet policy of korenizatsiya initially promoted local cadres but was abandoned by the late 1920s.
The official cultural formula became 'socialist in content, internationalist in spirit, national in form'.
In 1940, the Cyrillic script was forcibly introduced for the Uzbek language.
Mass deportations affected numerous ethnic groups, including Koreans, Meskhetian Turks, and Crimean Tatars.
During World War II, evacuation efforts relocated over 100 enterprises and 1 million people to Uzbekistan.
The title of Hero of the Soviet Union was awarded to 280 people from Uzbekistan, with 75 being Uzbeks.

data.heading: Post-Soviet Uzbekistan
bullets: Sharaf Rashidov: leader of the republic (1959-1983) who promoted industrial growth, irrigation, and cultural patronage
The Aral tragedy: consequence of uncontrolled withdrawal of Amu Darya and Syr Darya waters for cotton production
Perestroika: 'reconstruction' proclaimed by Gorbachev in April 1985
'New thinking': the foreign-policy doctrine of 'universal human values'
Cotton Affair: the 'Uzbek Affair' of 1983-1985 involving Gdlyan and Ivanov, with >25,000 arrested
Declaration of Independence: adopted on 18-20 June 1990, with 12 articles

narr: Sharaf Rashidov led Uzbekistan from 1959 to 1983, focusing on industrial development, irrigation projects, and cultural support.
The Aral Sea tragedy resulted from excessive water diversion from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers for cotton cultivation.
Perestroika, or 'reconstruction,' was initiated by Gorbachev in 1985 as part of broader Soviet reforms.
The 'new thinking' foreign policy emphasized universal human values in international relations.
The Cotton Affair of 1983-1985 led to the arrest of over 25,000 people, including officials Gdlyan and Ivanov.
Uzbekistan declared independence on June 18-20, 1990, establishing a framework with 12 articles.

data.heading: Independence and National Identity
bullets: GKChP: the State Committee for the State of Emergency; the coup of August 19, 1991
The Law 'On the Foundations of State Independence': adopted by emergency session on August 31, 1991
September 1: Independence Day of the Republic of Uzbekistan (since 1991)
Referendum on independence: nationwide vote in support of independence (December 1991)
The 'Uzbek model' / five principles: the nation's own path of development
State symbols: the emblem, flag, anthem as attributes of sovereignty under Constitutional Law

narr: The GKChP, or State Committee for the State of Emergency, attempted a coup against Gorbachev on August 19, 1991.
On August 31, 1991, an emergency session adopted the Law 'On the Foundations of State Independence'.
September 1 was established as Independence Day, celebrated annually since 1991.
A nationwide referendum in December 1991 confirmed public support for independence.
Uzbekistan developed its own path of known as the 'Uzbek model' based on five principles.
National symbols including the emblem, flag, and anthem were established as attributes of sovereignty.

narr: Our final question concerns the methods and principles used in the newest history of Uzbekistan.
The methods include historicism, which requires understanding events in their historical context.
The chronological method organizes historical events in time sequence.
The comparative method involves analyzing different historical phenomena side by side.
The statistical method uses quantitative data to support historical analysis.
The retrospective method examines past events from our present perspective.
These methods are guided by principles of scholarly rigor, objectivity, civilizational approach, and prioritizing the human factor.
